project_dependencies.use: PG37 owns the lexical examples at 26–27.
Frozen Kāśikā on 2.3.32 with the accusative verse.
Earlier rule and wind accusative control have zero repeat credit.
Full typed PG14 operator, histories and pairing.

source_observations.observation: Instrumental of the distinguishing quality underlies the two adjectives of a person known by it.

source_observations.locator: Bālā and Tattva 5.2.26, with the Kaumudī printed page
source_observations.observation: Retain pronounced initial c in both suffixes. Accounts appeal to the original teaching form or limited scope of the initial-marker rule.
Rāma, known for his weapons, speaks to Mārīca, known for his magic.

source_observations.locator: Jayamaṅgalā on Bhaṭṭi 2.32, stanza serial 59, printed p. 34
source_observations.observation: Explicitly supplies instrumental māyayā and astraiḥ. Mārīca and the speech are two accusative participants under a verb of speaking.
Separation qualifies the bases and the derivatives retain that meaning. Nyāsa assigns initial accent to the marker ñ.
Tattva explicitly gives the marker both grade and accent. Bālā distinguishes the base condition from an additional negation in the suffix.
Opens with an independent nānā. Sāyaṇa construes the different forms made by the pair as the objects of cakrāte.
Direct acute on the first syllable of the isolated word. The light and dark forms contrast in the following clause.
The same indeclinable has two different vowel junctions, before asti and iva.
Verse 1 has the longer nānānam. Verse 3 has a compound with dhī and the separate kin word nanā. Neither supplies the same independent word as RV 3.55.11.
Vinā and its first-person instrumental dependent mayā are separated by yat syāt in the verse.
The ordinary instrumental and ablative examples and the separately reasoned accusative are explicit. In this Kāśikā text the fourth wind-and-rain example has elephant-caused faults in the plural.

source_observations.locator: Harivaṃśa 51.29 in the Vaidya text, Brodbeck appendix 1
source_observations.observation: The parallel fourth phrase has a single elephant-caused fault in the accusative singular.
The spectators speak about the fallen trees. Drumau agrees with pātitau as the dual subject of their question.

source_observations.locator: Alastair Gornall, Rewriting Buddhism, discussion of 2.3.32
source_observations.observation: Independently identifies Harivaṃśa 51.29 and gives the grammatical version with the plural.
